--- title: "Item response models as neural networks" description: | The Rasch and 2PL models are tiny neural networks. Build them in PyTorch, widen the network, and ask whether it predicts held-out responses any better than the classical models, scored with the IMV on 27 IRW tables. format: html: code-fold: false toc: true toc-depth: 2 execute: echo: true eval: true message: false warning: false freeze: true --- A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch model takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an item, looks up one number for it ($d_i$, minus the difficulty), adds, and passes the sum through a sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden layer. The 2PL adds a second item lookup (the slope $a_i$). Once the models are written this way it is natural to ask what happens when the network is made wider or deeper: more latent dimensions, a nonlinear decoder. Does a neural network predict item responses better than the 2PL? This page builds the classical models in PyTorch, checks that they recover what the `mirt` package recovers, widens them, and scores every model on held-out responses from 27 IRW tables with the [InterModel Vigorish (IMV)](imv.qmd). Two more flexible one-dimensional models from R's `mirt` (the monotonic polynomial and an asymmetric item curve) are fit offline on the same split and join the comparison. ::: {#933c0858 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Setup"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import torch import irw from nn_irt_helpers import (TABLES, GROUPS, GROUP_OF, SHORT, prepare, fit, predict, imv, log_loss, make_models, SEED) Rasch, TwoPL, Bilinear, MLP = make_models() torch.set_num_threads(4) plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110 ``` ::: ## The models, written as networks The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes a batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit. | Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine | |---|---|---|---| | Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $d_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p + d_i$ | | 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, d_i$ (2) | $a_i\theta_p + d_i$ | | MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $d_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p + d_i$ | | MLP, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ | The models are written in slope-intercept form, $a_i\theta_p + d_i$, as `mirt` writes them, rather than the textbook $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$. That is not cosmetic. In the textbook form the gradient for $b_i$ is scaled by $a_i$, so difficulties of weak items barely move, and an $a_i$ kept positive by an exponential cannot fit an item keyed against the trait. Both bit this page in an earlier draft on the Woodworth inventory, which has 23 such items. The slope here is signed and unconstrained. The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL: $k$-dimensional person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which is also a low-rank matrix factorisation of the logit matrix. With $k=1$ it is the 2PL; the page uses $k=2$. The MLP concatenates the two embeddings and passes them through hidden layers of ReLU units, so the interaction between person and item is no longer constrained to be a dot product. This is the shape used in neural collaborative filtering. Two sizes are fit, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small one with a single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden layers of 64, so that depth is the only thing that changes. The next two sections build the 2PL from scratch, so that nothing is hidden; the full source of all four models and of the training loop is in [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py). ## Held-out cells, not held-out people Every one of these models has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a person it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people, test on others) is impossible. Instead we hold out **cells**: 20% of each person's responses, chosen at random, are hidden during training and predicted afterwards. Every person and every item stays in the training set. The same mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see the held-out cells as missing. The tables are all dense and dichotomous, and the response values are checked at fetch time rather than trusted from metadata. They were chosen to spread across the kinds of structure a wider network might find: tests built to measure one thing, knowledge tests whose items range over many topics, tests with a documented multidimensional structure, personality and clinical inventories that mix several syndromes or facets, and developmental screeners that span domains. Tables with more than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps with a fixed seed, so every fit on the page stays small. ::: {#b3e36420 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Fetch, subsample and split the tables"} data = {t: prepare(t) for t in TABLES} sizes = pd.DataFrame({SHORT[t]: {"group": GROUP_OF[t], "table": t, "persons": int(d.pid.max() + 1), "items": int(d.iid.max() + 1), "test cells": int(d.test.sum()), "mean resp": round(float(d.resp.mean()), 2)} for t, d in data.items()}).T sizes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `prepare` calls `irw.fetch`, caches the table, subsamples, assigns integer indices, and draws the mask with a fixed seed. Sizes are after subsampling. ## Building the network, step by step This section writes the 2PL as a network from nothing but `torch`, on one table, so that each piece can be seen. The helper module used for the comparison later is this code with bookkeeping added. ### 1. Long data is already the right shape A neural network consumes one training example at a time, and an item response is one example: a person index, an item index, a 0/1 outcome. Nothing has to be reshaped to a wide matrix. Three integer-coded columns become three tensors. ::: {#0253a869 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} d = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"] train = d[~d.test] P = torch.tensor(train.pid.values) # person index, 0..n_persons-1 I = torch.tensor(train.iid.values) # item index, 0..n_items-1 Y = torch.tensor(train.resp.values, dtype=torch.float32) # 0/1 response n_p, n_i = int(d.pid.max() + 1), int(d.iid.max() + 1) P[:5], I[:5], Y[:5], (n_p, n_i) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (tensor([1946, 506, 1335, 1109, 3172]), tensor([0, 0, 0, 0, 0]), tensor([0., 0., 0., 0., 0.]), (3223, 116)) ``` ::: ::: ### 2. An embedding is a lookup table of parameters `nn.Embedding(n, k)` is an `n x k` table of trainable numbers. Indexing it with a tensor of integers returns the matching rows. A person embedding of width 1 is a column of $\theta_p$; an item embedding of width 1 is a column of $d_i$. There is no "input layer" in the usual sense: the index *is* the input. ::: {#299c2d9e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import torch.nn as nn theta = nn.Embedding(n_p, 1) # one number per person theta.weight.shape, theta(P[:3]) # rows for the first three training cells ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (torch.Size([3223, 1]), tensor([[-1.8117], [ 0.8294], [ 0.6906]], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: ### 3. The forward pass is the item response function For the 2PL the logit is $a_i \theta_p + d_i$: look up three numbers and combine them. A `Module` packages the lookups and the combination, and the `forward` method is the item response function on the logit scale. The sigmoid that turns a logit into a probability is folded into the loss below, which is numerically safer than applying it here. ::: {#4e82f9f5 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} class TwoPLNet(nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_persons, n_items): super().__init__() self.theta = nn.Embedding(n_persons, 1) # person ability self.a = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) # item slope (signed) self.d = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) # item intercept (= -a * difficulty) nn.init.normal_(self.theta.weight, std=0.1) nn.init.ones_(self.a.weight) nn.init.zeros_(self.d.weight) def forward(self, p, i): return (self.a(i) * self.theta(p) + self.d(i)).squeeze(-1) net = TwoPLNet(n_p, n_i) logits = net(P[:5], I[:5]) logits, torch.sigmoid(logits) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (tensor([ 0.0223, 0.1986, -0.1153, -0.0474, 0.0593], grad_fn=), tensor([0.5056, 0.5495, 0.4712, 0.4882, 0.5148], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: At initialisation every item has slope 1 and intercept 0 and every person is near 0, so every probability is about one half. ### 4. The loss is the negative log-likelihood `BCEWithLogitsLoss` is $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_c \big[y_c \log p_c + (1-y_c)\log(1-p_c)\big]$ with $p_c = \sigma(\text{logit}_c)$: the mean negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, which is exactly the quantity an IRT package maximises. Before training it is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$, the log-loss of a fair coin. ::: {#ab79d7dc .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0.6942863464355469 ``` ::: ::: ### 5. A prior on persons, because persons are parameters Fitting a free $\theta_p$ for every person by maximum likelihood is joint maximum likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons grows and runs away for perfect scores. IRT software avoids this by integrating $\theta$ out under a $N(0,1)$ prior (marginal maximum likelihood). The network's equivalent is to add $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_p \theta_p^2$ to the loss, scaled by $1/n$ to match the mean log-likelihood. That makes the fit a MAP estimate under the same normal prior, and it is a single line. ::: {#b41ab506 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} def objective(net, p, i, y, n=len(train)): nll = loss_fn(net(p, i), y) prior = 0.5 * (net.theta(p) ** 2).sum() / n # N(0,1) prior on theta return nll + prior ``` ::: (The helper module spreads the prior over each person's responses so that it is unbiased in a minibatch; the idea is the same.) ### 6. The training loop Gradient descent on the objective, in minibatches, with Adam as the optimiser. Each pass over the training cells is an epoch. This is the whole algorithm; everything else is monitoring. ::: {#ead8a3e3 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} torch.manual_seed(SEED) opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=0.02) n, batch = len(train), 4096 for epoch in range(10): perm = torch.randperm(n) for s in range(0, n, batch): j = perm[s:s + batch] opt.zero_grad() objective(net, P[j], I[j], Y[j]).backward() opt.step() with torch.no_grad(): print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d} train log-loss {loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item():.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` epoch 1 train log-loss 0.5572 epoch 2 train log-loss 0.5430 epoch 3 train log-loss 0.5409 epoch 4 train log-loss 0.5402 epoch 5 train log-loss 0.5399 epoch 6 train log-loss 0.5398 epoch 7 train log-loss 0.5398 epoch 8 train log-loss 0.5397 epoch 9 train log-loss 0.5397 epoch 10 train log-loss 0.5397 ``` ::: ::: Ten epochs take a few seconds on a laptop CPU, and the training log-loss settles at the value the 2PL can reach on this table. Held-out predictions are the same forward pass on the held-out indices, through a sigmoid: ::: {#25ac8fed .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} test = d[d.test] with torch.no_grad(): p_test = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(test.pid.values), torch.tensor(test.iid.values))).numpy() log_loss(test.resp.values, p_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 0.5479447465771263 ``` ::: ::: That is a complete item response model, fit by a neural-network toolkit, in about thirty lines. The Rasch model drops the slope. The multidimensional model makes the embeddings wider. The MLP replaces the dot product with hidden layers. All four live in the helper module with the same training loop (`fit`), which also records train and held-out loss per epoch. ## Checking against mirt ::: {#d5583ca4 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} rasch, h_rasch = fit(Rasch(n_p, n_i), d) twopl, h_2pl = fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d) h_rasch.tail(1), h_2pl.tail(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` ( epoch train test 79 80 0.54951 0.557622, epoch train test 79 80 0.539586 0.547848) ``` ::: ::: Does the network recover the item parameters? The offline R `mirt` 2PL fit (marginal maximum likelihood on the same training cells; see below) wrote its slopes and intercepts next to its predictions, so compare. ::: {#0924ef05 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ref = pd.read_csv("nn_irt_data/borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt_mirt_2pl_items.csv", dtype={"item": str}) ref = ref.set_index("item").reindex(sorted(d["item"].unique())) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4)) ax[0].scatter(ref.d, twopl.d.weight.detach().numpy().ravel(), s=12) ax[0].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL intercept $d$", ylabel="PyTorch 2PL intercept $d$") sd_theta = twopl.theta.weight.detach().numpy().std() ax[1].scatter(ref.a, twopl.a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel() * sd_theta, s=12) ax[1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL slope $a$", ylabel=r"PyTorch 2PL slope $a \times \mathrm{sd}(\hat\theta)$") for a_ in ax: lo, hi = a_.get_xlim(); a_.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=978 height=428} ::: ::: The intercepts agree to the dot. The slopes agree once the scale of $\theta$ is accounted for: `mirt` fixes the *population* variance of $\theta$ at one, while the network's point estimates are shrunk by the prior and have a smaller spread, so its raw slopes are proportionally larger. Multiplying them by the spread of $\hat\theta$ puts the two on the same footing. The remaining scatter is the difference between a point estimate for each person and integrating the person out, which the next section returns to. ## Widening the network Now the models that are not classical IRT. Train-versus-test log-loss by epoch makes the overfitting visible: once the test curve turns up, further training is memorising the training cells. ::: {#e0ce56a6 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} curves = {} curves["Rasch"] = h_rasch curves["2PL"] = h_2pl _, curves["MIRT k=2"] = fit(Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), d, epochs=30) _, curves["MLP small"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), d, epochs=30) _, curves["MLP large"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), d, epochs=30) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=False) for name, h in curves.items(): ax[0].plot(h.epoch, h.train, label=name) ax[1].plot(h.epoch, h.test, label=name) ax[0].set(title="training log-loss", xlabel="epoch", ylabel="log-loss") ax[1].set(title="held-out log-loss", xlabel="epoch") ax[1].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=979 height=429} ::: ::: ## Scoring with the IMV The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet: if model 0 predicts held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and model 1 as well as a coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the relative gain in the bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the definition and the R package; here it is in Python. ::: {#829cc222 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import inspect print(inspect.getsource(imv)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` def imv(y: np.ndarray, p0: np.ndarray, p1: np.ndarray) -> float: """InterModel Vigorish of model 1 over model 0 on held-out cells.""" w0 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p0)) w1 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p1)) return (w1 - w0) / w0 ``` ::: ::: Fit every model on every table. Each PyTorch model is trained for 80 epochs with the epoch of lowest held-out loss reported (early stopping, with the held-out set doing double duty as validation set; a production comparison would carve a third split). The `mirt` fits come from [`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R), run offline on the same split. ::: {#53430b31 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Fit all PyTorch models on all tables"} from pathlib import Path def best_epoch_preds(model_fn, d, epochs=30): """Train, keep the predictions from the epoch with lowest held-out loss.""" te = d[d.test] best = (np.inf, None) model = model_fn() hist = [] for ep in range(epochs): model, h = fit(model, d, epochs=1, seed=SEED + ep) p = predict(model, te) ll = log_loss(te.resp.values, p) hist.append(ll) if ll < best[0]: best = (ll, p) return best[1] nn_specs = { "Rasch": lambda n_p, n_i: Rasch(n_p, n_i), "2PL": lambda n_p, n_i: TwoPL(n_p, n_i), "MIRT k=2": lambda n_p, n_i: Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), "MLP small": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), "MLP large": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), } preds = {} for t, d in data.items(): n_p, n_i = d.pid.max() + 1, d.iid.max() + 1 te = d[d.test] preds[t] = {"y": te.resp.values} for name, mk in nn_specs.items(): preds[t][name] = best_epoch_preds(lambda: mk(n_p, n_i), d) mp = Path("nn_irt_data") / f"{t}_mirt_preds.csv.gz" if mp.exists(): m = pd.read_csv(mp, dtype={"id": str, "item": str}) m = te[["id", "item"]].merge(m, on=["id", "item"], how="left") for c in m.columns: if c.startswith("mirt_"): preds[t][c] = m[c].values ``` ::: ::: {#c32ed632 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="IMV chart"} rows = [] for t, pr in preds.items(): y = pr["y"] for name, p in pr.items(): if name in ("y", "2PL") or np.isnan(p).all(): continue rows.append({"table": t, "model": name, "log-loss": log_loss(y, p), "IMV vs 2PL": imv(y, pr["2PL"], p)}) res = pd.DataFrame(rows) order = [m for m in ["Rasch", "MIRT k=2", "MLP small", "MLP large", "mirt_2pl", "mirt_monopoly", "mirt_lpe"] if m in set(res.model)] labels = {"mirt_2pl": "mirt 2PL", "mirt_monopoly": "mirt monotonic poly.", "mirt_lpe": "mirt LPE"} imv_tab = res.pivot(index="table", columns="model", values="IMV vs 2PL").reindex(TABLES)[order] # tables grouped, and within a group ordered by the MIRT gain group_colour = dict(zip(GROUPS, ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#2f9e6e", "#8e5bd6", "#c9a227"])) rows_order = [] for g, ts in GROUPS.items(): ts = [t for t in ts if t in imv_tab.index] rows_order += sorted(ts, key=lambda t: -imv_tab.loc[t, "MIRT k=2"]) imv_tab = imv_tab.reindex(rows_order) ypos = np.arange(len(rows_order))[::-1] lim = float(np.nanmax(np.abs(imv_tab.values))) * 1.1 fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(order), figsize=(13, 0.32 * len(rows_order) + 1.6), sharey=True) for ax, m in zip(axes, order): ax.barh(ypos, imv_tab[m], color=[group_colour[GROUP_OF[t]] for t in rows_order], height=0.7) ax.axvline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8) ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim) ax.set_title(labels.get(m, m), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7) ax.grid(axis="x", color="0.9", lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True) for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False) axes[0].set_yticks(ypos, [SHORT[t] for t in rows_order], fontsize=8) axes[0].set_xlabel("IMV relative to PyTorch 2PL", fontsize=8, loc="left") from matplotlib.patches import Patch fig.legend(handles=[Patch(color=c, label=g) for g, c in group_colour.items()], loc="lower center", ncol=3, fontsize=8, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.01)) plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1)); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=1419 height=1029} ::: ::: Each panel is one model; each bar is one table, coloured by the kind of instrument and grouped so that the groups can be compared. Bars to the right of zero mean the model predicts held-out responses better than the PyTorch 2PL on that table (the 2PL is the zero line, so it has no panel). The `mirt` panels are R's `mirt` fit by marginal maximum likelihood on the same training cells, with each held-out cell predicted by its posterior-predictive probability (the item curve integrated over the person's posterior): the 2PL again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the monotonic polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function rather than a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent model (LPE), whose item curve is asymmetric. The last two change the *shape* of the item curve while keeping one latent dimension, which is the opposite move from the networks above. ::: {#11550599 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The numbers: IMV vs 2PL and held-out log-loss"} ll2 = pd.Series({t: log_loss(pr["y"], pr["2PL"]) for t, pr in preds.items()}, name="2PL") ll_tab = res.pivot(index="table", columns="model", values="log-loss").reindex(rows_order)[order] ll_tab.insert(0, "2PL", ll2.reindex(rows_order)) out = pd.concat({"IMV vs 2PL": imv_tab.round(4), "held-out log-loss": ll_tab.round(4)}, axis=1) out.index = [SHORT[t] for t in out.index] out ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Four things stand out. **On tests built to measure one thing, nothing beats the 2PL.** Across the achievement and ability tests, the knowledge tests and the two exams with a documented multidimensional structure, the wider networks sit within about 0.01 IMV of the 2PL, and as often below it as above. The ECPE grammar test is the instructive case: it has a known three-attribute Q-matrix, and a model built to find structure still predicts no better, because the attributes are too correlated to carry separate signal in held-out cells. The one clear exception in this group is the FSIQ mental-rotation test, where every wider network gains about 0.03, which says the test is not unidimensional in practice whatever it was built to measure. **Where the networks win, the win is multidimensionality, and the 2-D MIRT captures it as well as the MLPs do.** The gains cluster in the personality and clinical inventories: about 0.03 on the ADQ anhedonia scale, 0.02 on the Eysenck EPI (three scales in one table), 0.008 on the Woodworth, with smaller gains on the Author Recognition Test and the GMI. In every one of these the MLPs match or trail the MIRT, and the large MLP is never reliably better than the small one. Once the embeddings are two-dimensional, a nonlinear decoder adds nothing on these data: depth is not where the signal is. The Rasch panel shows the same thing from the other side. Its large losses (0.11 on the NPI, 0.08 on the ADQ, 0.07 on the Denver screener) are tables where slopes differ sharply across items, including reverse-keyed items a Rasch model cannot fit at all. **The flexible item curves add nothing.** The asymmetric LPE curve tracks the `mirt` 2PL to within 0.001 on every table. The monotonic polynomial is the same on the tests and worse on several inventories (0.04 below on the NPI, 0.015 on the ADQ), and it failed to converge on three of the longer tables. Changing the shape of the item curve while keeping one dimension is not where the predictable signal is either. **The `mirt` 2PL column is an estimator effect, and it is largest on short tests.** The same 2PL fit by marginal maximum likelihood beats the gradient descent fit by 0.03 on the 25-item COVID knowledge test, 0.009 on the 30-item ENCCEJA and the 18-item financial literacy test, and by nothing on the 116-item residency exam. With a free slope per item, a normal prior on $\theta$ alone does not bound the product $a_i\theta_p$: trained to convergence the network's slopes grow and its person estimates shrink (their spread is 0.4 on the short tests against 0.56 on the residency exam), and held-out loss climbs. Early stopping is what keeps the network's 2PL honest here, and it is not quite enough when each person has only 20 responses. Integrating $\theta$ out, as marginal maximum likelihood does, removes the problem; a prior on the slopes would blunt it. The page leaves the network as it is so that the effect is visible, and the comparison to read is therefore networks against the PyTorch 2PL (same estimator) and flexible curves against the `mirt` 2PL (same estimator). ## What this page does not do The networks here see only person and item identities, exactly as the classical models do, so this is a comparison of functional forms, not of information. Models that use more information are a different question: sequential models of learning (knowledge tracing) use the order of responses; models with item text as input can predict items never seen in training; variational IRT replaces the point estimates with an encoder network that amortises person scoring, which is also the principled fix for the estimator gap above. All of them can be scored with the same held-out cells and the same IMV. ## Further reading - Wu, Davis, Domingue, Piech & Goodman (2020), "Variational item response theory: fast, accurate, and expressive", *EDM*. - He, Liao, Zhang, Nie, Hu & Chua (2017), "Neural collaborative filtering", *WWW*. - Domingue, Kanopka, Stenhaug, et al.
